 Appearance:
 Shri Yogesh Kumar Gupta - Advocate for the appellant.
 Shri Manas Mani Verma - Public Prosecutor for the responden
ORDER Per: Justice Vivek Agarwal With the consent, heard at motion stage.

This appeal is filed under Section 374(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure being aggrieved of the judgment dated 14/11/2022 passed by the learned Special Judge (POCSO Act) 2012 Waraseoni,
District Balaghat in Special Case No. 23/2019 whereby the learned trial Judge has convicted appellant Sanjay Pandhre under Section 376 (2)(n) of I.P.C. with ten years R.I. and fine of Rs. 200/-
with default stipulation of one month Simple Imprisonment.

Similarly, he has been convicted for offence under Section 5(l)(j)(ii) r/w Section 6 of POCSO Act 2012 with twenty years R.I. and fine of Rs. 200/- with default stipulation of one month Simple Imprisonment.
It is submitted that another accused namely Jeevanlal Pandhre father of the present appellant too was made an accused.
He was acquitted by the NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-JBP:55346 2 CRA-10971-2022 learned trial court.
It is submitted that the prosecution case in short is that prosecutrix PW-1 is the resident of village Tekadi.
She failed in X th class and, therefore, was learning household work.
Appellant Sanjay is son of her aunt and was frequently visiting her house.

In August 2018, he gave a proposal for marriage Sanjay Pandhre vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 8 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/160102133/
1 and after two days at the instance of the appellant, she informed her family members that she is going to the house of her friend.

sentences.text: At about 8 P.M., she reached the house of Indra Bai where appellant met her.
He took her on his motorcycle to village Pipariya and on the next day, they travelled to Gondia by train and from Gondia to Hyderabad where they lived together.
She became pregnant and was carrying 2 1 / 2 months of pregnancy.
When in February 2019, the appellant brought her to village Pipariya and after staying for eight to ten days, he went back to Hyderabad.
It is submitted that testimony of the prosecution is silent on use of force or any other coercion.
Reading from the evidence of the prosecutrix PW-1, it is pointed out that she has not supported the prosecution case and was declared hostile.
PW-2 is father of the victim.
He has stated that her daughter was born in the year 2000.
In the Examination-in-Chief, he has admitted that at the time of the incident, when his daughter had left her home, she was 18 years of age.
PW-3 mother of the victim too has turned hostile and has not supported the prosecution case.
As per prosecution, the date of birth of the prosecutrix is 10/11/2001 and, therefore, she was minor at the time of the incident.

On the contrary, NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-JBP:55346 3 CRA-10971-2022 PW-10 Dilip Kumar Kurha, Incharge Headmaster, Government Primary School has stated that in the school records, date of birth of the prosecutrix is mentioned as 10/11/2001 but in the cross-examination, this witness has admitted that date of birth was written orally as per the instructions of father of the prosecutrix and no documentary evidence like Kotwari record,
Anganwadi record and Panchayat record etc.was enclosed or brought by him to support the date of birth of the prosecutrix.

Thus, it is submitted that in view of such evidence, since date of birth of the prosecutrix is doubtful,
her Xth class certificate is not seized and there is ambiguity in the statements of PW-10, in the light of the judgment of the Supreme Court in Birad Mal Singhvi Vs. Anand Purohit AIR 1988 SC 1796 that when there is discrepancy and the prosecution has failed to prove the date of birth of the prosecutrix to show her to be minor at the time of the incident, then benefit should accrue in favour of the appellant.
Shri Manas Mani Verma, learned Public Prosecutor opposes the prayer and submits that the appellant is already married to the prosecutrix.

sentences.text: They have a small child.
There is no justification in allowing the appeal.
Benefit of doubt is a double edged sword and it can cut either way.

After hearing learned counsel for the parties and going through the record, it is evident that the Supreme Court in the case of Birad Mal Singhvi (supra) has held that Section 35 of the Evidence Act provides that to make a document admissible, three conditions must be satisfied.
Firstly, entry that is related must be one in a public or other official book, register or record.

sentences.text:
Secondly, it must be an entry stating a fact in issue or relevant fact and NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2024:MPHC-JBP:55346 4 CRA-10971-2022 thirdly, it must be made by a public servant in discharge of his official duty or any other person in performance of a duty as would be enjoined by law.

An entry relating to date of birth made in the school register is relevant and admissible under Section 35 of the Act but the entry regarding age of the person made in a school register is not of much evidentiary value to prove the age of the person.
In the absence of the material on age, the basis of which was recorded, this entry cannot be taken as sacrosanct.
In the present case, as per the evidence of PW-10 Incharge Headmaster, age of the prosecutrix was recorded on the dictates of father of the prosecutrix.
PW-2 father of the prosecutrix has admitted that he is illiterate and he does not remember the date of birth of the prosecutrix.
He has categorically stated that when prosecutrix left his home, she was 18 years of age.
There is no contradiction to this part of the evidence and the same is the fact in regard to the evidence of mother of the prosecutrix PW-3.
Therefore, when material fact in regard to the entry of date of birth is not proved through other documentary or oral evidence, then benefit of doubt needs to be accrued in favour of the appellant.
Thus, when examined, then counsel for the appellant has been able to demonstrate that there is doubt as to the minority of the prosecutrix at the time of the incident.

Her father has himself admitted that she was major at the time of the incident, then it will become a consensual act as submitted by Shri Yogesh Kumar Gupta, learned counsel for the appellant and admitted by Shri Manas Mani Verma in the district of Balaghat and adjoining districts.
NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-JBP:55346 5 CRA-10971-2022
This marriage between a daughter of Mama and son of Bua is an accepted norm.
Therefore, in view of such facts and when prosecution has failed to prove that prosecutrix was minor on the date of the incident, provisions of Section 5/6 of POCSO Act will not be applicable.

In the case of consent, provisions of Section 375 of I.P.C. too is also not applicable justifying the conviction under Sections 376 (2) (n) of I.P.C. and 5(l)(j)(ii) r/w Section 6 of the POCSO Act and the consequent sentence.
Therefore, the appeal deserves to be allowed and is allowed.
The impugned judgment of conviction is set aside.
The appellant, if not required in other case be set free.
In above terms, the appeal stands allowed and is disposed of.
